micro_skills.grade_rationale: At Grade 2, students are developing fine motor skills and symbolic representation. Drawing and simple modeling are age-appropriate methods for expressing complex ideas, building on their natural inclination to draw and play.
micro_skills.knowledge_object: design ideas for a purposeful artifact
misconceptions: Drawings must be perfect or artistic.

micro_skills.pedagogical_rationale: This micro-skill is foundational for the design process, enabling students to externalize and share their initial thoughts before physical construction. It fosters creativity and early communication skills essential for collaborative work.
required_resources: Optional: Simple modeling materials (e.g., play-doh, construction paper, glue, scissors)
micro_skills.statement: Communicate design ideas for a purposeful artifact using drawings or simple models.
success_criteria: The drawing clearly shows the shape and main features of the container.
The student can explain how the container will hold pencils.
The design shows an understanding of the container's purpose.
teaching_sequence: Diagnosis: Ask students to draw a 'house for a toy'. Observe clarity and detail.
Practice: Introduce examples of simple design drawings (e.g., a chair, a box). Guide students to draw their own ideas for a simple object, focusing on purpose.
Feedback: Provide constructive feedback on clarity and how well the drawing communicates the intended purpose. Encourage peer feedback.

micro_skills.pedagogical_rationale: This skill is crucial for translating design ideas into physical reality. It develops practical dexterity, problem-solving, and an understanding of material properties and tool functions, all while emphasizing safety.
required_resources: Various craft materials (cardboard, paper, fabric scraps, pipe cleaners)
micro_skills.statement: Select and safely use appropriate materials and tools to construct a simple artifact.
success_criteria: The student selects materials appropriate for the artifact's purpose (e.g., sturdy for structure, flexible for decoration).
The student uses tools (e.g., scissors, glue) safely and correctly.
The constructed artifact resembles the design and holds together.
teaching_sequence: Diagnosis: Observe students' prior experience with scissors, glue, and construction. Ask them to identify safe ways to use these.
Practice: Demonstrate safe handling of each tool and material. Provide guided practice sessions where students experiment with joining different materials.
Feedback: Circulate during construction, providing immediate feedback on tool safety and material selection. Highlight good practices and correct unsafe habits.

micro_skills.accessibility_support: Provide sentence starters or visual prompts for evaluation (e.g., 'My container is good at...', 'My container needs to be...'). Allow verbal responses or drawing improvements for students with writing difficulties.
micro_skills.assessment_task: After constructing their pencil container, students will test if it holds pencils effectively. They will then explain what works well and what could be improved, suggesting one change.
micro_skills.evidence_limitations: The evidence supports the general idea of evaluating products against design criteria but does not specify the complexity of criteria or the depth of evaluation expected from Grade 2 students.
micro_skills.evidence_of_mastery: Student can articulate whether their artifact fulfills its purpose and propose at least one relevant modification to improve it.

evidence_quotes.quote: evaluate their ideas and products against design criteria

micro_skills.grade_rationale: At Grade 2, students can begin to make simple judgments about functionality. This skill encourages them to think beyond just 'making' to 'making well' and introduces the concept of criteria-based assessment.
micro_skills.knowledge_object: a constructed artifact against its intended purpose
misconceptions: My artifact is perfect and cannot be improved.
Only the teacher can say if something is good or bad.
micro_skills.pedagogical_rationale: Evaluation is a critical step in the design cycle, teaching students to reflect critically on their work and understand that design is iterative. It fosters problem-solving and continuous improvement.
required_resources: Pencils or other items to test the artifact's purpose
micro_skills.statement: Evaluate a constructed artifact against its intended purpose and suggest simple improvements.
success_criteria: The student tests the artifact's functionality (e.g., puts pencils in the container).
The student identifies at least one aspect that works well or doesn't work well.
The student suggests a simple, relevant improvement (e.g., 'make it taller', 'add a lid').
teaching_sequence: Diagnosis: Ask students to describe what makes a good chair. Observe their ability to identify functional criteria.
Practice: Provide examples of simple products and discuss how well they meet their purpose. Guide students to test their own artifacts and articulate observations.
Feedback: Facilitate a class discussion where students share their evaluations and proposed improvements. Emphasize that 'failures' are opportunities for learning.

initial.rationale: This unit introduces Grade 2 students to the fundamental stages of the design process: ideation, creation, and evaluation. By focusing on purposeful artifacts, students learn to connect their designs to real-world needs. The progression from drawing ideas to hands-on construction and critical reflection builds essential problem-solving and practical skills. The micro-skills are designed to be atomic and durable, ensuring a strong foundation for future technological education.
initial.safety_notes: All activities involving tools must be conducted under strict adult supervision. Only child-safe scissors and non-toxic glues should be used. Emphasize proper handling and storage of all materials. For any future activities involving circuits, only low-voltage batteries (e.g., AA, AAA) are permitted, and direct supervision is mandatory; never use mains electricity. Paper-based circuit activities are for conceptual understanding and do not imply real electrical operation.
initial.title: Design a purposeful artifact

plan.learning_goal: Identify a need, sketch and make an artifact, and evaluate it against its intended purpose.
plan.progression: Move from identifying a need to testing and improving a simple design.
plan.retrieval_query: design make evaluate purpose materials tools
plan.title: Design a purposeful artifact

issues.finding: The micro-skill 'select-and-use-materials-tools' does not list any prerequisites. To construct an artifact from a design, the design must first be created. This creates a logical gap in the pedagogical sequence.

issues.correction: Remove the text concerning electrical circuits from the 'safety_notes' to align them with the unit's actual scope. The note should focus exclusively on the safe use of the listed materials (scissors, glue, etc.).
issues.finding: The 'safety_notes' section includes a detailed warning about electrical circuits, including low-voltage batteries and mains electricity. This content is irrelevant to the proposed unit, which focuses on simple craft materials like paper and cardboard.

issues.correction: Integrate a brief, hands-on exploration of the properties of the provided materials within this unit's teaching sequence, rather than assuming it as a prerequisite from Science.
issues.finding: The micro-skill 'select-and-use-materials-tools' lists 'Basic properties of materials (e.g., strength, flexibility) from Science' as external knowledge. This assumes prior learning from another subject area which may not be guaranteed.

strengths: The unit provides a clear and logical introduction to the design process (ideate, make, evaluate) that is well-suited for the target grade level.
Each micro-skill is supported by relevant evidence from the provided curriculum sources.
The proposed assessment tasks are concrete, observable, and directly aligned with the learning objectives of each micro-skill.
The inclusion of specific accessibility supports for each micro-skill demonstrates a commitment to inclusive design.
The identification of common misconceptions for each skill is a valuable resource for teachers, allowing them to proactively address potential learning barriers.
